X.1.title: In his village, at court
X.1.reflection: Book X is different: it describes the Master's manner rather than recording his sayings. In his home village he was simple and almost wordless; at the ancestral temple and at court he spoke fluently, but with care. The same man adjusted his speech to the place.
X.1.question: How does your speech change between home and work?

X.2.title: Speaking with officers
X.2.reflection: With officials of lower rank he spoke freely and straight; with higher ones, mildly but precisely; in the ruler's presence, respectful and composed. The book records how rank shaped the tone of speech in his world.
X.2.question: With whom do you speak more freely, and with whom more carefully?

X.3.title: Receiving a guest
X.3.reflection: When the ruler asked him to receive a guest, his face changed and his step quickened; he bowed left and right, robe straight before and behind, and hurried forward like a bird with spread wings. When the guest was gone, he reported: the guest no longer looks back. A ceremonial duty, described in minute detail.
X.3.question: What duty do you perform with complete attention to its form?

X.4.title: Through the palace gate
X.4.reflection: Entering the palace gate he bent as if it were too low; he did not stand in the middle of the gateway or step on the threshold. Passing the ruler's empty seat, his face changed, and he spoke as if short of breath. Coming out, a step down, he relaxed. Reverence is described in the body, step by step.
X.4.question: Is there a place where you change your manner as you enter?

X.5.title: Carrying the jade tablet
X.5.reflection: Carrying the ruler's jade tablet on a mission, he bowed as if it were too heavy, held it at a precise height, walked with short steps. At the presentation of gifts he was composed; at the private meeting, pleased. Each stage of a mission had its proper face.
X.5.question: What carries more weight than it physically has, when you hold it?

X.6.title: His clothes
X.6.reflection: The junzi did not use dark purple or puce for trimmings or red for everyday clothes; he matched outer robes to furs, wore a long night robe, and changed dress for mourning and for the new moon. Book X keeps details of dress because dress was part of ritual. The list reads as foreign now, and that is its value: a picture of how one man lived inside his customs.
X.6.question: What do your own clothes say about the occasions in your life?

X.7.title: When fasting
X.7.reflection: Before a sacrifice, during the fast, he wore clean linen, changed his food and changed where he sat. Preparation for a rite began days before it, in small changes of daily habit.
X.7.question: How do you prepare, in small ways, for something important?

X.8.title: At the table
X.8.reflection: He did not mind fine rice or finely cut meat, but would not eat food that was spoiled, discoloured, badly cooked or out of season; he wanted it cut properly and with its sauce; he did not let meat exceed the rice; he set no limit to wine but never became confused; he always had ginger; he did not eat much; he did not talk while eating. Even a plain meal began with a small offering. The longest chapter of Book X is about eating with care.
X.8.question: What would change if you ate one meal today with full attention?
X.8.exercise: Eat one meal today without talking or looking at a screen, and notice it.

X.9.title: A straight mat
X.9.reflection: If his mat was not straight, he did not sit on it. Seven words in Legge. Order in small things was a habit of attention.
X.9.question: What small thing do you set straight before you begin?

X.10.title: The elders leave first
X.10.reflection: At village drinking, he left only after those with staffs, the elders, had left. When villagers performed the exorcism ceremony, he stood in court dress on the eastern steps. He kept village custom as seriously as court ritual.
X.10.question: Which local customs do you respect, even if you do not share them?

X.11.title: Medicine he did not know
X.11.reflection: Sending greetings to someone in another state, he bowed twice to the messenger. When Ji Kangzi sent him medicine, he accepted it with a bow but said: I do not know it, so I dare not taste it. Courtesy and caution together.
X.11.question: How do you accept a gift you cannot use?

X.12.title: Was anyone hurt?
X.12.reflection: The stables burned. Returning from court, he asked: was anyone hurt? He did not ask about the horses. Horses were costly and the grooms were of low status, which is why the question is remembered.
X.12.question: In a loss, what do you ask about first?

X.13.title: Gifts from the ruler
X.13.reflection: When the ruler sent cooked food, he straightened his mat and tasted it first; raw meat, he cooked and offered to his ancestors; a live animal, he kept alive. Ill in bed when the ruler came, he lay with his head east, court robe over him. Summoned, he went on foot without waiting for his carriage. Every contact with the ruler had its form.
X.13.question: Who in your life would you go to at once, without waiting?

X.14.title: Asking about everything, again
X.14.reflection: In the Grand Temple, he asked about everything. The line of III.15 returns, without the sneer and the reply. Book X keeps the habit itself.
X.14.question: Where could you ask more questions than you do?

X.15.title: I will bury him
X.15.reflection: When a friend died with no one to take care of him, he said: let me see to the burial. He did not bow for a friend's gift, even a carriage, except for sacrificial meat. Friendship had its own duties, the last of them the most binding.
X.15.question: What would you do for a friend that no one would ask of you?

X.16.title: Thunder and wind
X.16.reflection: He did not sleep like a corpse or sit at home as if at a ceremony. He changed his face at the sight of mourners, of officials, of the blind; he bowed in his carriage to those in mourning and to bearers of census records; at a lavish feast he rose; at sudden thunder or a great wind his expression changed. Respect for others, and for the forces of the sky.
X.16.question: What still makes your expression change?

X.17.title: In the carriage
X.17.reflection: Mounting his carriage he stood straight and held the cord; inside, he did not look around, speak fast or point. Composure even in transit.
X.17.question: How do you carry yourself when you are on the way somewhere?

X.18.title: The pheasant on the bridge
X.18.reflection: A bird rises at the sight of people, circles and settles. The Master says: the pheasant on the hill bridge, how timely, how timely! Zilu makes a gesture toward it, and it sniffs three times and flies. The fragment is obscure, and the text may be damaged. It is often read as praise of acting at the right moment, which closes a book about manners.
X.18.question: What did you do today at exactly the right moment?
